Innovation variances that force a unit diagonal

Source: R/dag_layer.R
mc_dag_unit_diagonal.Rd

Returns the innovation variances under which the covariance of the directed layer has unit diagonal, that is under which it is a correlation matrix, and says whether the coefficients supplied admit them.

Usage

mc_dag_unit_diagonal(gamma, R, edges = NULL)

Arguments

gamma

finite numeric vector of structural coefficients, exactly one per edge.

R

a single positive integer, the number of responses.

edges

optional integer matrix with columns \((i, j)\), \(i < j\), the directed edges \(i \to j\). If NULL, the complete DAG on the natural ordering \(1 < 2 < \dots < R\) is used. Each edge must occur exactly once; duplicated rows, including reversed duplicates, are rejected because they do not define distinct structural coordinates. A row given as \((j, i)\) with \(j > i\) is read as the same edge \(i \to j\): the direction always follows the natural order of the responses. The rows are sorted lexicographically before use, and gamma is read in that sorted order, not in the order the rows were supplied. Sort the matrix yourself, or read the order back from the edges component of the result, whenever the correspondence matters.

Value

A list with delta, the innovation variances implied by the coefficients; admissible, true when all of them are positive; min_delta; Sigma_b, the covariance they produce, which has unit diagonal when admissible; r_squared, the variance of each response accounted for by its parents; and to_unit_innovations, the diagonal rescaling that sends the covariance to the representative of its orbit with unit innovations.

Why this is a constraint and not a reparametrization

The undirected layer can fix the diagonal at one at the cost of nothing. Here the requirement $$\delta_j=1-\boldsymbol\gamma_j^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{b,P_jP_j} \boldsymbol\gamma_j,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \delta_1=1,\quad\delta_j=1-\sum_{k<j}L_{jk}^2\delta_k,$$ with \(\mathbf L=\mathbf T^{-1}\), leaves \(|E_D|\) free parameters but confines them to the open set where every \(\delta_j\) stays positive, a set defined by \(R\) nonlinear inequalities. It contains the origin and is a proper subset of the coefficient space whenever there is an edge. That is exactly the freedom the layer buys by leaving the diagonal free, which is why the fitting routines do not impose it: the constraint is useful for reading a covariance as a correlation and for reproducing a generator, not for estimating.

One representative per orbit

Rescaling by \(\mathbf A\) sends \(\delta_j\) to \(a_j^2\delta_j\), so every orbit \(\{\mathbf A\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\mathbf A\}\) contains exactly one matrix with unit innovation variances, reached by \(a_j=\delta_j^{-1/2}\). The component to_unit_innovations carries that rescaling.

See also

mc_dag_coefficients for the scale-free quantities.

Other directed layer: mc_build_D_matrix(), mc_build_T_matrix(), mc_cholesky_derivatives(), mc_cholesky_to_covariance(), mc_cholesky_to_precision(), mc_dag_closed_root(), mc_dag_coefficients(), mc_dag_sensitivity()

Examples

# a chain: the second and third responses keep less and less of their own
mc_dag_unit_diagonal(c(0.6, 0.6), R = 3, edges = rbind(c(1, 2), c(2, 3)))$delta
#> [1] 1.00 0.64 0.64
# coefficients too large for a correlation matrix are flagged
mc_dag_unit_diagonal(c(0.9, 0.9), R = 3,
                     edges = rbind(c(1, 3), c(2, 3)))$admissible
#> [1] FALSE
